Review 1: Major focus. Argues that the paper uses a \(P=.01\) threshold justified as \(0.05/5\) for the Big Five even though, in the Add Health analysis discussed, there were about 90 tests, and many more candidate variables were available. It frames this as a broader “spaghetti at the wall” problem. (Red Team of Science)
Review 2: Also catches multiplicity, but elsewhere. It identifies roughly 130 primary directional MR tests (plus negative controls) conducted without formal multiplicity correction, under a permissive “2 of 3 estimators” rule.
Comparison / what one caught that the ot: Agreement on the general problem; different evidence. R1 catches the outcome-screening / Add Health multiplicity that R2 largely misses. R2 catches the MR-specific multiplicity problem that R1 does not analyze.

Issue: Selective reporting / researcher degrees of freedom
Review 1: Central criticism. Notes that only a subset of available associations receives narrative emphasis, while plausible null or contradictory outcomes go unmentioned; points to examples such as suspension vs. expulsion, imprisoned father vs. own imprisonment, etc. It also argues the p-value distribution in Figs. 2B/3 is suggestive of selection. (Red Team of Science)
Review 2: Does not really develop this critique. It audits what is reported and finds many inconsistencies, but does not ask systematically whether the chosen outcomes represent a selected subset of a much larger analysis universe.
Comparison / what one caught that the ot: Important R1-only point. R2’s detailed audit does not substitute for R1’s “garden of forking paths” / selective-outcome concern.

Review 1: Major focus. Argues that enormous sample sizes make minuscule effects statistically significant and potentially headline-worthy; emphasizes that some reported associations correspond to very small absolute differences. (Red Team of Science)
Review 2: Mostly does not criticize effect sizes for being practically trivial. Its discussion of precision is more about technical interpretation—for example, low precision of AFR-like estimates.
Comparison / what one caught that the ot: R1-only. Review 2 is much more concerned with validity of estimates than with whether statistically valid effects are scientifically meaningful.

Review 1: Implied by its broader concern that many weak associations are elevated into noteworthy findings, but it does not dissect the MR methods.
Review 2: Very strong critique. Notes that 29 of 33 claimed MR relationships are significant only under weighted-median/mode analyses while MR-CAUSE intervals include zero; also raises correlated pleiotropy and sample-overlap concerns.
Comparison / what one caught that the ot: R2 catches much more. This is one of Review 2’s strongest additions.

Issue: Whether different personality instruments really measure a common genetic construct
Review 2: Questions the “only one heterogeneous locus” claim because the Genomic SEM model first adds 11 data-driven cross-loadings, some substantial, before calculating \(Q_{\mathrm{SNP}}\).
Comparison / what one caught that the ot: R2-only. A technically important qualification to one of the paper’s headline robustness claims.

Review 2: Questions the paper’s unconstrained linear correction of SNP heritability for scale reliability: the fitted model implies nonzero heritability at zero reliability, whereas classical measurement-error logic suggests a proportional relationship. It also questions the \(SE^{-1}\) weighting.
Comparison / what one caught that the ot: R2-only. This gets at whether the paper’s higher “reliability-corrected” heritability numbers are well justified.

Review 2: Finds the general within-family result impressive but flags caveats: \(r_g<1\) for neuroticism and agreeableness, attenuation for openness, and ambiguity in how “96.2% of variance” is described. The review further notes that those percentages are ratios of regression coefficients, not proportions of \(R^2\).
Comparison / what one caught that the ot: R2-only. This materially qualifies one of the manuscript’s main “minimal confounding” claims.

Review 2: Questions unspecified sibling/cousin-to-spouse scaling formulas, effects of split-half \(r_g=0.94\), and interpretation of very small genetic mate correlations.

Comparison / what one caught that the ot: R2-only. This is a scope-of-inference criticism rather than a multiple-testing one.

Extensive. Finds 14-vs-17 prior extraversion loci, conflicting sample sizes, twin-pair vs. individual counts, 50,725 vs. 55,637 within-family \(N\), figure/caption mismatches, citation errors, corrupt reporting-summary text, and numerous smaller errors.

Review 1: Mostly skeptical; the huge sample size is treated partly as what permits trivial effects to become significant.
Review 2: Explicitly credits the study’s scale, multi-ancestry GWAS, within-family triangulation, psychometric analyses, and breadth of outcomes as genuine strengths.
Comparison / what one caught that the ot: Different emphasis rather than contradiction. R1 asks whether scale magnifies questionable discovery practices; R2 treats scale/design breadth as strengths while scrutinizing implementation.

Issue: Interpretation of “1,000+ variants linked to personality”
Review 1: Argues that the media-level formulation is too strong, partly because the broader analytic environment is insufficiently multiplicity-controlled and effects are tiny. (Red Team of Science)
Review 2: Does not challenge the 1,260 genome-wide-significant lead SNPs themselves on standard GWAS multiplicity grounds; instead it finds specific inconsistencies in locus counts and follow-on analyses.
Comparison / what one caught that the ot: This is an important distinction: R1 sometimes blurs the standard GWAS discovery threshold with the multiplicity problem in downstream exploratory analyses. R2 is more compartmentalized statistically.

Review 1: Argues that nominal corrections cannot account for all analyses researchers could choose to run across many authors, outcomes, transformations, and datasets. (Red Team of Science)
Review 2: Mostly evaluates the documented analysis plan/results, not the unknowable universe of analyses that might have been attempted.
Comparison / what one caught that the ot: R1-only conceptual point. Whether you find it persuasive depends on how much evidence you require before inferring undisclosed analytic selection.
